samples.text:
The chart shows the global revenue from recorded music in four formats, which are CD, vinyl, downloads and streaming, in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025.

In 2010, CD was the most popular format with $8.4 billion. Downloads was second with $4.2 billion, but streaming and vinyl was very small, only $0.4 billion and $0.2 billion.

After that, CD revenue fell a lot. It went down to $4.6 billion in 2015, $1.8 billion in 2020 and only $1.1 billion in 2025. Downloads also decreased, from $4.2 billion to $3.9 billion in 2015, and then it dropped to $0.5 billion in 2025.

On the other hand, streaming increased very fast. In 2015 it was $2.9 billion but in 2020 it jumped to $13.4 billion, and in 2025 it reached to $20.8 billion, which is the highest figure in the chart. Vinyl also grow, from $0.2 billion to $2.1 billion, so in 2025 it was more than CD.

Overall, streaming became the main format for music, while CD and downloads became less important.
samples.why: Main trends identified and figures accurate · overview short and placed last · format-by-format listing with basic linking · some imprecise word choice · agreement and verb-form errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The bar chart illustrates worldwide revenue from recorded music in four different formats at five-year intervals between 2010 and 2025.

Overall, there was a dramatic shift from physical and downloaded music towards streaming, which grew to dominate the market. Revenue from CDs and downloads declined significantly, whereas vinyl saw steady growth.

In 2010, CDs generated the largest income, at $8.4 billion, twice as much as downloads ($4.2 billion), while streaming and vinyl brought in less than half a billion dollars each. Over the following fifteen years, CD revenue fell continuously, dropping to $4.6 billion in 2015 and to only $1.1 billion by 2025. Downloads followed a similar downward path, although the decline was slow at first, from $4.2 billion to $3.9 billion, before accelerating to reach just $0.5 billion in 2025.

Streaming, by contrast, grew enormously. From a mere $0.4 billion in 2010, it rose to $2.9 billion in 2015 and then jumped to $13.4 billion in 2020, making it the leading format. By 2025 it had reached $20.8 billion. Vinyl sales also increased steadily over the period, climbing from $0.2 billion to $2.1 billion and overtook CDs in the final year.
samples.why: Clear overview of the shift to streaming · key trends well highlighted with accurate figures · logical progression and a range of linkers · some less common vocabulary · one minor verb-form slip.

samples.text:
The chart tracks global revenue from four recorded music formats, CD, vinyl, downloads and streaming, at five-yearly intervals from 2010 to 2025.

The period was marked by the spectacular rise of streaming, which went from a negligible source of income to overwhelmingly the largest. Revenue from CDs and downloads contracted sharply, while vinyl, despite remaining a relatively small format, enjoyed sustained growth.

In 2010, CDs were the principal source of revenue, earning $8.4 billion, double the figure for downloads ($4.2 billion). Both formats subsequently declined, though at different rates: CD income fell steadily to $1.1 billion by 2025, whereas downloads held up reasonably well until 2015, at $3.9 billion, before collapsing to $1.2 billion in 2020 and a mere $0.5 billion in 2025.

Streaming revenue, meanwhile, rose from just $0.4 billion in 2010 to $2.9 billion in 2015, and then surged to $13.4 billion in 2020, exceeding all the other formats combined. By 2025 it had reached $20.8 billion, more than fifty times its initial level. Vinyl followed a more modest but equally consistent upward trend, increasing more than tenfold from $0.2 billion to $2.1 billion and eventually outperforming CDs.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected with accurate derived multiples · clear, well-placed overview · contrasting trends linked fluently · wide, precise vocabulary · wide range of structures, error-free.
